title: Black Panther
subtitle: The mantle in main Marvel continuity — T'Challa, and Shuri while she wore it
blurb: 350 issues from his first guest spots to the 2024 finale, in the order they're meant to be read.
notes: 1 is the readable path — McGregor, Priest and Coates, and nothing else. 2 is strongly recommended: Hudlin's run, the Kasper Cole stretch that ends Priest's, Ridley, Ewing, and the six issues that finish the Klan story. 3 is genuinely optional. The minimum viable path is Tier 1 alone.

All of this is main Marvel continuity — no Ultimate line, no what-ifs, no 2099. And the list follows the mantle rather than the man: Shuri is the Black Panther for the 2009 volume and Doomwar, so those issues are in, the same way every T'Challa volume is.
The Fantastic Four issues are not here, on purpose.

He debuts in Fantastic Four #52–53 and returns in #54, #56 and #119. Those rows live on the Fantastic Four list in this catalogue; duplicating them would give one issue two ids and two sets of ticks. The 2006 stretch where T'Challa and Storm stand in on the team is different — those are Black Panther issues, and they are in.

Sections link to their Marvel series pages rather than to each issue, because Marvel only exposes the 20 most recent issues of a series to the outside world. The issue numbers tell you when to switch titles.

Issue ranges machine-read from Wikipedia's Black Panther collected editions tables, with Jungle Action's own article for the vol. 2 range and the reprint at #23, and Eve Ewing's bibliography for the ninth volume. Every row is attested by a collected edition that names it; the generator refuses to emit one that is not. Series links resolve against Marvel's own series ids.

sections.title: Before the solo book
sections.sub: 1968 into the 1970s — guest spots in other people's comics
sections.intro:
This is Marvel's own Black Panther: The Early Marvel Years omnibus, minus the Fantastic Four issues. He debuts in Fantastic Four #52–53 and comes back in #54, #56 and #119 — those rows are on the Fantastic Four list in this catalogue, and copying them here would give the same issue two sets of ticks.

What is left is guest appearances in other people's books, so they are grouped by title the way the omnibus lists them rather than shuffled into one timeline. Nothing below depends on having read any of it.

sections.title: Panther's Rage
sections.sub: 1973–1975 — thirteen issues, and where the run actually starts
sections.intro:
Don McGregor was proofreading everything Marvel published when he pointed out that a comic called Jungle Action, set in Africa and starring white adventurers, was indefensible. Marvel gave him the book on one condition — keep it in Africa — and he handed it to the Black Panther.

What he wrote is thirteen issues of one continuous story, planned and finished as a whole, which almost nobody in American superhero comics was doing in 1973. It is where Erik Killmonger comes from, and it is what every later writer goes back to. Start here.

items.note: “Panther's Rage” begins — McGregor, Buckler and Billy Graham
The chapters get longer here, 18 to 19 pages

sections.title: Panther vs. the Klan
sections.sub: 1976 — five issues, and no ending
sections.intro:
McGregor's second arc, and it does not finish: Jungle Action was cancelled at #24 with the story mid-flight. Marvel reasoned the character could still sell with a new approach, which is the next section.

There is no #23 below because #23 is not a new chapter — it is a reprint of Daredevil #69, which is already in the section above. The ending this arc eventually got is two sections down.

items.note: “Panther vs. the Klan” begins
The last issue — the title was cancelled with the arc unfinished

sections.title: The Kirby run
sections.sub: from January 1977 — the co-creator's own thing, and it ignores everything above
sections.intro:
Marvel relaunched the character in his own title with Jack Kirby — back from DC — writing, drawing and editing it. Kirby was not continuing McGregor. He was not continuing anything: it is twelve issues of Kirby at full volume, built around an artefact hunt, and it connects to nothing on either side of it.

That is the honest answer to where it sits. It is Tier 3, it is in publication order because that is the only order it has, and skipping it costs you nothing later.

items.note: Kirby writing, drawing and editing

sections.title: Where the Klan story ends
sections.sub: 1979–1980 — three years late, and by a different writer
sections.intro:
Kirby left after twelve issues. Ed Hannigan and Jerry Bingham took the last three, picked the abandoned Klan subplot back up — and were cancelled in turn, so the conclusion ran in Marvel Premiere, an anthology title, later the same year.

McGregor wrote none of it. It is Tier 2 anyway, because it is the only ending those five Jungle Action issues have.

items.note: Ed Hannigan writing, Jerry Bingham pencilling
The Klan story is picked back up as a subplot
Where the Klan story finally ends, in an anthology title

sections.title: The wilderness years
sections.sub: 1988–1991 — a miniseries, an anthology serial and a prestige book
sections.intro:
Nine years with no ongoing title, and then three things that are not one: a four-issue miniseries by Peter B. Gillis and Denys Cowan; “Panther's Quest”, which is McGregor again, published as twenty-five eight-page chapters inside the biweekly anthology Marvel Comics Presents and set in apartheid South Africa; and “Panther's Prey”, McGregor with Dwayne Turner.

The Marvel Comics Presents rows are eight pages each, not whole issues. After this the character does not carry a book again until 1998.

items.note: Peter B. Gillis and Denys Cowan

sections.title: Priest: The Client
sections.sub: 1998–2000 — the run everyone means
sections.intro:
Christopher Priest inherited a character with a reputation as a dull also-ran and rebuilt him as a head of state: Wakanda as a sovereign technological power, T'Challa as its king first and an Avenger a distant second, and a State Department attorney called Everett Ross narrating so that the reader has somebody to be.

It is also, structurally, a political comedy. The first issue is deliberately hard to follow and the run spends sixty-two issues explaining itself. Coates calls this the classic run; if you read one Black Panther comic, read this one.

items.note: Priest and Mark Texeira, under the Marvel Knights imprint

sections.title: Priest: Enemy of the State
sections.sub: 2000–2001 — the run at full tilt
sections.intro:
The middle stretch, and the point at which the shape of the thing becomes clear. Storm comes back into the book at #25.

The Deadpool issue at the end is the other half of a crossover, collected inside the run by Marvel's own omnibus. It is optional.

items.note: Storm comes back into the book
The Deadpool half of a crossover — collected inside the run

sections.title: Priest: the last stretch
sections.sub: 2001–2003 — fourteen issues before the book changes lead
sections.intro: The title kept changing shape to survive, and Priest kept writing it. These are the last fourteen issues with T'Challa as the lead.

sections.title: Kasper Cole
sections.sub: the end of the Priest run — thirteen issues in which T'Challa is the supporting cast
sections.intro:
The last thirteen issues of Priest's run replace the lead. Kasper Cole is a New York police officer in a costume he has no claim to, and T'Challa is a supporting character in his own title.

Same writer, same run, same ending — which is why it is Tier 2 rather than optional. But if you are here for T'Challa, this is where he is least present.

items.note: Kasper Cole takes the lead; T'Challa becomes a supporting character

sections.title: The Crew
sections.sub: 2003 — the spin-off, cancelled at seven
sections.intro: Priest again, running alongside the final Black Panther issues and cancelled with #7. Kasper Cole is in it.

items.note: Ran alongside the last Black Panther issues
Cancelled here

sections.title: Hudlin: Who is the Black Panther?
sections.sub: 2005–2006 — the restart that outsold Priest
sections.intro:
Reginald Hudlin started the book over from the beginning with John Romita Jr. drawing, retelling the origin for people who had never picked the character up. It sold better than any Black Panther comic before it, Priest's included.

It reads nothing like Priest — broader, louder, and much more interested in T'Challa as a global player than as a puzzle. The House of M tie-in and the X-Men crossover are inside the run rather than bolted onto it.

sections.title: Hudlin: the Civil War years
sections.sub: 2006–2008 — twenty issues and the annual
sections.intro: The middle of the run goes straight through Marvel's Civil War, and then spends five issues — “Four the Hard Way” — with T'Challa and Storm standing in for two absent members of the Fantastic Four. Those are Black Panther issues, so they are here; the Fantastic Four's own issues from those months are on the Fantastic Four list.

sections.title: Secret Invasion
sections.sub: 2008 — three issues by somebody else
sections.intro: Jason Aaron closes the fourth volume with a war story tied into the line-wide Skrull event. Three issues, and then the book stops.

items.note: Jason Aaron takes over for the last three

sections.title: Shuri wears the mantle
sections.sub: 2009–2010 — the fifth volume, and it is not T'Challa's
sections.intro:
Hudlin again, with T'Challa's sister Shuri as the Black Panther. Jonathan Maberry co-writes #7 and takes the book from there.

The list follows the mantle rather than the man, which is why twelve issues with a different person under the mask are in it.

items.note: Shuri's book — Hudlin scripting
Jonathan Maberry co-writes, then takes the book

sections.title: Doomwar
sections.sub: 2010 — six issues, plus a four-issue side book
sections.intro: A crossover miniseries with the Fantastic Four and the X-Men in it, and the hinge between the Shuri book and where the character spends the next two years. Klaws of the Panther is a separate four-issue series from the same months and is marked optional.

items.note: With the Fantastic Four and the X-Men in it

sections.title: The Man Without Fear
sections.sub: 2011–2012 — Daredevil's numbering, Daredevil's neighbourhood
sections.intro:
T'Challa takes over Daredevil's title at #513 and Daredevil's patch of New York with it: no Wakanda, no vibranium, a diner in Hell's Kitchen and a false name. David Liss writes; Francesco Francavilla draws the first stretch.

The title becomes The Most Dangerous Man Alive at #524 and the numbering carries straight on. #523.1 is a point-one issue and sits where its number says it does.

sections.title: A Nation Under Our Feet
sections.sub: 2016–2017 — Coates and Brian Stelfreeze
sections.intro:
Ta-Nehisi Coates' first twelve issues, and the book the modern character is built on. It opens by asking whether a country should have a king at all, from inside the king's head, and it does not let him off easily.

It assumes almost nothing. If you want a starting point later than 1973, this is the other one.

items.note: Coates and Brian Stelfreeze

sections.title: Avengers of the New World
sections.sub: 2017–2018 — and the renumbering that lands mid-arc
sections.intro: The second Coates arc, interrupted by Marvel's legacy renumbering: #18 is followed by #166, which is the same run counting from the character's first appearance in 1966 instead of from 2016. Nothing changes but the number on the cover.

items.note: Marvel's legacy numbering — the same run, counting from 1966

sections.title: The Intergalactic Empire of Wakanda
sections.sub: 2018–2021 — twenty-five issues, in space
sections.intro:
Coates' second volume is a space opera, and it is a harder sell than the first: it starts a long way from Wakanda and takes its time telling you why. It is also where he finishes what he started.

Read it after the first volume. It does not work cold.

items.note: Coates again, with a new number one

sections.title: Around the Coates run
sections.sub: 2016–2019 — five spin-offs, none of them load-bearing
sections.intro:
Books that ran alongside. World of Wakanda is Coates with Roxane Gay on the Dora Milaje; Black Panther and the Crew is Coates again, on a police-killing story in Harlem; Long Live the King and Shuri are both Nnedi Okorafor; Rise of the Black Panther goes back to the early years.

The main run does not refer back to any of them.

sections.title: John Ridley
sections.sub: 2021–2023 — fifteen issues, and it is a spy story
sections.intro:
Ridley's run is espionage: a king with an intelligence service, and what he has been using it for. Juann Cabal draws the first arc.

It follows Coates directly and reads better for it.

items.note: John Ridley and Juann Cabal

sections.title: Eve Ewing
sections.sub: 2023–2024 — ten issues, and the last ongoing so far
sections.intro:
Eve Ewing and Chris Allen — the first Black woman to write the book. Ten issues.

This is the end of the list, not the end of the story. Anything newer than this is not here yet.
